title: The Night Watch isn’t a night scene, and it was cut down to fit a wall
body: Rembrandt’s 1642 group portrait is really titled Militia Company of District II under the Command of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq. The nickname came later, when layers of **dark varnish** made the daylight scene look nocturnal; the varnish came off only in the 1940s. In 1715 the canvas was moved to Amsterdam Town Hall and trimmed on all four sides, presumably to fit between two columns. A 17th-century copy by Gerrit Lundens preserves the lost composition, and in 2021 the painting was shown with the missing strips recreated by neural networks from that copy.

left.label: The nickname
left.text: The Night Watch: a misnomer that stuck once darkened varnish made the scene look like night.

right.text: Militia Company of District II under the Command of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq, 1642.

slides.question: How wide is the Night Watch today, in centimetres?
slides.explanation: 437 cm wide and 363 cm tall, even after it was trimmed in 1715. By area, almost 40 Mona Lisas would fit on the canvas.

slides.label: the painting’s size today, after the 1715 trimming
slides.text: It belongs to the Amsterdam Museum but hangs in the Rijksmuseum as the best-known painting in its collection.

slides.heading: Restored in public
slides.text: The painting was attacked with a knife in 1975 and sprayed with acid in 1990. In July 2019 a long restoration began inside a specially built glass enclosure in the museum, so that visitors could watch the work.

slides.heading: Four centuries of the Night Watch
slides.note: The dark varnish that earned the nickname came off in the 1940s.

slides.heading: Earliest first
slides.explanation: Completed in 1642, trimmed in 1715, cleaned of its varnish in the 1940s, and shown with AI-recreated edges in 2021.
